from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        lecture_lines = [

        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Dimensional Paradox", lecture_lines)

        # Assets/Objects

        self.place_at_grid(square, 'B5', scale_factor=0.8)
        self.play(Create(line_segment), Create(square))
        self.lecture[0].set_color(BLUE)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(self.lecture[1]))
        self.place_in_area(animation_group, 'B2', 'D5', scale_factor=0.75)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(self.lecture[2]))
        self.place_at_grid(animation_group, 'C3', scale_factor=0.7)
        self.play(Indicate(square))
        self.lecture[2].set_color(GREEN)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(self.lecture[3]))
        curve = VGroup(*[Dot(self.grid[f"{r}{c}"], radius=0.05, color=RED) for r in "BCDE" for c in "345"])

        self.lecture[3].set_color(RED)
        
        self.wait(2)

            "Recursion creates infinite complexity."

sections.title: The Dimensional Paradox (0:00-0:45)
sections.content: Introduce the prerequisite concept: A 1D line has length, and a 2D plane has area. Pose the question: Can a continuous line pass through every single point in a 2D square? Challenge the intuition that a line has 'zero area'.
sections.example: Visualize a thin thread moving across a square grid; show how it can never fill the 'gaps' until it infinitely twists.

sections.title: The Peano Curve Construction (0:45-2:00)
sections.content: Explain the recursive algorithm. Start with a square grid (1x1), subdivide into 9 smaller squares, and trace a path through them. Show that as the iteration count 'n' approaches infinity, the path effectively covers all points.
sections.example: An animation of a 'snake-like' path subdividing into smaller segments, demonstrating how complexity increases with each iteration step.

sections.title: The Hilbert Curve: Efficiency in Recursion (2:00-3:15)
sections.content: Introduce the Hilbert curve as a more popular alternative to Peano. Explain the 'L-shape' rotation logic. Emphasize that it is continuous, surjective, and maintains locality (points close together on the line are close in the 2D space).
sections.example: A visual comparison: Hilbert curve vs. a random scribble, showing how the Hilbert curve maps a 1D sequence to a 2D layout without 'jumping' across distant areas.

sections.title: Real-World Applications (3:15-4:30)
sections.content: Explain why this matters: Database indexing (mapping 2D geographical data to 1D disk storage), image processing, and fractal antenna design. Explain that 'locality' helps computers read data faster.
sections.example: A 'Pixel-sorting' robot character moving along a Hilbert path to organize scattered colored dots into a coherent image efficiently.

sections.title: Conclusion and Intuitive Summary (4:30-5:00)
sections.content: Summarize the key takeaway: Space-filling curves are infinite limits of simple patterns that allow us to 'flatten' dimensions. Encouraging students to see fractals as nature's way of maximizing surface area.
sections.example: A final graphic showing a human lung or a fern leaf, highlighting how nature uses space-filling principles to pack maximum surface area into minimal volume.
